extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, dramatists, and informed readers of Romantic-era literature
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for dramatic and poetic works (especially tragedy) drawn from Coleridge's literary criticism: what makes a tragedy morally and artistically appropriate, how stagecraft and diction affect reception, and how critics should substantiate judgments. Emphasis is on moral representation, character-consistency, style, and performative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of sin and moral consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient drama presents guilty passion not as the immediate subject to be made interesting but in its consummation — 'livid, ghastly, and appalling' — and directs attention to the consequences and punishment of criminal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Orestean trilogy (avenging and punitive focus), Medea (punishment of Jason). Guidance: tragedy should represent sin after its consummation, emphasizing consequences and moral lesson rather than making sinful emotion itself attractive. Anti-pattern: treating guilt or crime as the point of sympathetic interest, thereby offending decency or inflaming criminal passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appealing to lowest emotions / sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The corrupt drama . . . exhibits what is essentially base in a form as interesting as it can be made to assume' — it arrays mean and contemptible things 'in a glittering veil of sentiment' and appeals to the lowest, most excitable parts of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings and examples: contemporary French dramatists accused of 'polluting the public mind' by stimulant displays of atrocities and vileness in odious detail. Guidance: dramatists should not dress up gross material to excite sensational feeling; the play's power should not rest on low emotional stimulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject choice must be appropriate to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's choice of subject should lie within 'the legitimate range of tragedy' and be justifiable by precedent; error may be unconscious but subject still needs principled justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/questioning: Bertram's subject may have seemed within tragic precedent to its author but nevertheless errant in effect. Guidance: evaluate whether the subject invites tragic treatment and whether precedent supports its moral and aesthetic handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches and images must cohere with a character's established voice and preceding/following discourse; isolated, incongruous passages (e.g., Imogine's lines borrowed from Lear and Dryden) indicate bad construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: moments that 'stand unique in the speeches of [a character], without the lightest resemblance to anything she says before or after.' Guidance: check characters for believable continuity in manner, tone, and diction; sudden revolutions in manner risk audience confusion (e.g., Prior's abrupt change of manners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid senseless plagiarism and incongruent borrowings
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing lines, images, or modes from other celebrated works in a way that is senseless or incongruous weakens a drama (e.g., plagiarism from Lear and Dryden inserted without relation to the speaker or context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two lines in Imogine are 'senseless plagiarism' from Lear and a 'senseless adoption' of Dryden's forest fiend. Guidance: allusion and influence must be organic and appropriate to voice and situation; jarring or isolated borrowings are aesthetic faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft: ensure audibility, visibility, and credible mise-en-scène
rubrics_metrics.description: Staging choices must allow the audience to perceive essential elements: props, music, and stage pictures must be appropriate and perceivable (criticizes a 'phantom' altar, boys singing on stage, dark woods back-scene which the audience cannot hear or fully see).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chorister boys actually sung on stage though much of audience had 'small chance of hearing a word'; elaborate scenic devices that are merely phantasmagoric. Guidance: consider practical theatre realities — sightlines, audibility, and whether stage effects serve the drama rather than distract or confuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve important plot elements and personages
rubrics_metrics.description: Key personages and plot-pieces (e.g., a child introduced as important) must be accounted for; failure to resolve their fate makes the work feel incomplete or riddling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the child in Bertram is 'an important personage' — the critic insists there was 'no possible means' of ending the acts without its final appearance. Guidance: ensure that vital threads are tied up or intentionally left unresolved with clear artistic purpose; unexplained riddles are a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glorifying villainy or presenting immoral acts as heroic
rubrics_metrics.description: A drama should not reward or dignify loathsome actions by granting villains nobility or piety at the close (e.g., Bertram's last exclamation and prayer following heinous crimes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bertram, a 'loathsome and leprous confluence' of crimes, petitions monks to pray and dies with a warrior's boast — this is morally incoherent. Guidance: maintain moral proportion; do not present criminals' acts in ways that might be read as admirable or exculpatory without clear critical framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics must substantiate moral charges with textual evidence and regard audience moral sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges that a work is immoral have effect only insofar as they are substantiated by the play itself and by the auditors' moral sense; unsubstantiated personal attacks are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to critics: provide textual basis for charges, avoid merely personal or political invective. The critic notes that a charge 'could have no effect except just so far as it was substantiated by the play itself, and the moral sense of its auditors.' Anti-pattern: vague denunciation without demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/recitation strongly shapes reception
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner and force of a performer or reciter can create or amplify audience sympathy; a warm, celebrated reciter can lend his will and apprehension to auditors and change reception of a poem or scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the enkindling reciter, by perpetual comment of looks and tones, lends his own will and apprehensive faculty to his auditors.' Guidance: authors and performers should be aware that oral delivery can mask or highlight textual qualities; readings can create temporary sympathy not necessarily reflecting text's independent merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of prejudice in reception: personal enmity, partisan and market pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Reception can be distorted by private enmity, political faction, or the commercial need for saleable abusive reviews; authors may be prejudged (e.g., labeled 'metaphysical') before fair appraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Coleridge's works were reviewed with malignity and 'predetermined insult' influenced by politics and private animus. Guidance: critics/readers should discount ad hominem and partisan motives; authors should expect and account for possible prejudgment in reception and marketing of works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, diction, and style must suit thought and subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and diction should be consistent with the author's thought-world: classical simplicity suits certain poets (Casimir), while heterogeneous thoughts produce barbarized diction (Cowley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: Casimir's classical diction vs Cowley's 'barbarized' Latin and metre. Guidance: align diction and metrical choices to intellectual stance and subject matter; mismatches weaken poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility: maintain proportionality of cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative and critical clarity arises from perceiving a proportion between antecedents and consequents; confusion or unintelligibility causes distress and weakens effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From conclusion: the mind is 'so framed' that confusion is painful; making grief intelligible (opening out our griefs) brings alleviation. Guidance: in storytelling and argument, ensure causal relations and intelligible structure to give the reader/audience comfort and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate moral exposure from purely literary censure when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining moral denunciation with literary criticism can weaken the moral effect; the critic should consider treating moral exposure and literary faults distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author expresses 'dislike to the literary censures which accompany the moral exposure, because I think they tend to weaken its effect.' Guidance: when addressing moral failings, weigh whether literary censure aids or distracts from moral argument; choose the mode that strengthens the intended corrective.
